Full text

Abstract

Purpose Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = -2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = -0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = -0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = -0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

Introduction

Anxiety and other mental health problems have increased substantially among U.S. college students over the past two decades (Duffy et al., 2019; Nails et al., 2023). These difficulties can interfere with academic performance, interpersonal relationships, and quality of life, yet many students experiencing psychological distress do not receive formal treatment (Eisenberg et al., 2011; Lipson et al., 2022). Thus, there is a need for brief and scalable interventions that can be administered before psychological difficulties become severe. Fear of negative evaluation (FNE), defined as apprehension about and concern over others' negative judgments, may be a particularly important target for early intervention in college populations.

Cognitive and neurobiological research identifies FNE as a core feature of social anxiety disorder (Birk et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2025). Social-evaluative fears may be especially consequential during college, where academic participation, relationship formation, and entry into new social networks frequently involve interpersonal evaluation; elevated social anxiety symptoms have accordingly been associated with functional impairment and poorer academic achievement among university students (Brook & Willoughby, 2015; Dell'Osso et al., 2014). Importantly, social-evaluative fears vary dimensionally and can interfere with functioning across a broad range of symptom severity, suggesting that the consequences of FNE and related concerns extend below the diagnostic threshold (Busch et al., 2023; Dell'Osso et al., 2014; Ruscio et al., 2008). Thus, FNE represents both a central feature of social anxiety disorder and a dimensional cognitive vulnerability relevant to student mental health and well-being.

Cognitive models propose that social-evaluative fears are maintained partly by maladaptive interpretations of social situations. Individuals with elevated social anxiety may overestimate the likelihood or consequences of negative social outcomes, assume that visible anxiety or imperfect performance will lead to rejection, and evaluate themselves according to excessively demanding standards (e.g., Clark & Wells, 1995; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). Particularly relevant to the present study, they may treat unfavorable evaluation as highly consequential or intolerable and devote substantial effort to controlling how they are perceived (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). These appraisals can promote maladaptive threat-focused anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, self-focused attention, and avoidance (Clark & Wells, 1995; Mellings & Alden, 2000; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). Daily-process research illustrates how these mechanisms operate among college students: on days characterized by greater FNE, students also report greater maladaptive anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, and social withdrawal (Campbell et al., 2016), which in turn may form a self-reinforcing pattern. Maladaptive anticipatory processing can heighten anxiety before and during a social encounter when it involves repetitive predictions of embarrassment or rejection, negative self-imagery, and doubts about one's ability to manage an unfavorable outcome, with little corresponding focus on constructive ways of responding to possible difficulties (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hinrichsen & Clark, 2003). Meanwhile, post-event rumination can sustain distress, exacerbate social anxiety symptoms, and strengthen negative expectations (Clark & Wells, 1995; Edgar et al., 2024). Moreover, although withdrawal can provide shortterm relief, it ultimately limits opportunities to learn that unfavorable outcomes may be manageable and that effective action remains possible despite uncertainty (Hofmann, 2007). Because FNE is linked to these proximal cognitive and behavioral processes, it is a promising target for preventive intervention.

A growing literature has evaluated brief and scalable cognitive-behavioral approaches to social anxiety and FNE among college students, although evidence for reductions in broad FNE and generalization to acute social-evaluative responding remains mixed. Established cognitivebehavioral interventions address social anxiety by helping individuals examine catastrophic predictions, reduce attempts to control how they are perceived, redirect attention away from internal threat monitoring, and engage with feared situations despite uncertainty (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007). Digitally delivered approaches provide a potentially scalable means of making these strategies available to college students (Harrer et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2023). Internet-based CBT has been found to reduce social anxiety symptoms among university students relative to a waitlist control (McCall et al., 2018; Kählke et al., 2019), with one such study also reporting a significant between-group reduction in broad FNE (McCall et al., 2018). Similarly, a six-session smartphone-based hypnosis intervention produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE among undergraduates with elevated shyness than a no-treatment control (Ma et al., 2024). Brief face-to-face approaches provide additional evidence that FNE may be modifiable over relatively short periods, including a three-day intensive group CBT program that produced reductions in FNE relative to a waitlist control (Cui & Tang, 2026). These studies help establish brief and digital interventions for FNE as promising in college students, but one important limitation of the above-mentioned digital intervention studies is the use of a waitlist or no-treatment control.

Brief intervention and digital intervention studies that have used an active (rather than waitlist or no treatment) control have found inconsistent effects on FNE, and evidence for reductions in broad FNE among college students remains especially limited. In an RCT of a brief in-person intervention comparing six-session group exposure and response prevention with an educational-support active control among college students, FNE changes did not differ significantly between conditions, despite a significant intervention effect on social anxiety (Zaboski et al., 2019). Project Engage, a self-guided digital single-session intervention designed to help college students cope with FNE in active-learning science courses, increased immediate confidence in small-group and whole-class participation; however, broad FNE was assessed only at baseline, and outcomes were classroom-specific (Ghosh et al., 2023). Online Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretation (CBM-I) has also been examined as a preventive intervention during the transition to college. Among students anxious about beginning university, five online CBM-I sessions produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE from baseline to the first day of university than an expectancy-matched active control involving neutral visuospatial brain-training tasks (Hoppitt et al., 2014). This finding demonstrates that a brief online intervention can reduce FNE in anticipation of the transition to university; however, because training occurred before the semester and the between-condition difference was not significant four weeks later, it remains unclear whether comparable effects would emerge or remain evident when an intervention is delivered amid ongoing academic and social-evaluative demands (Hoppitt et al., 2014). More recently, in a community sample of adults with elevated social anxiety that was not specific to college students, a six-session online CBM-I led to a significantly greater decrease in FNE relative to an active control when measured one week after the end of the intervention period (although the between-group effect immediately after training narrowly missed significance) (Abado et al., 2026). Thus, brief and scalable interventions have shown promise, but evidence remains limited regarding whether a scalable digital intervention with broader cognitive targets can produce between-group reductions in broad FNE in college students, particularly when comparing to an active control and when delivered amid ongoing academic and social-evaluative demands.

Stoic training may provide a promising broad cognitive approach to decrease FNE in college students, but to our knowledge the effects of Stoic training on FNE have yet to be evaluated. Although the word "stoic" is colloquially used to refer to suppression of emotional expression and has historically been used similarly in portions of the psychological literature, philosophical Stoicism encourages awareness of emotional reactions and deliberate examination of the judgments that shape them (Karl et al., 2022; LeBon et al., 2026; Murray et al., 2008; Pathak et al., 2017; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). Thus, philosophical Stoicism emphasizes understanding and regulating emotion rather than denial or suppression (Karl et al., 2022; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026). Preliminary evaluations conducted by the Modern Stoicism organization have reported within-group pre-to-post-intervention improvements in well-being, resilience, and Stoic attitudes following large-scale online programs such as Stoic Week and Stoic Mindfulness and Resilience Training, although these findings are limited by self-selection, attrition, the absence of control conditions, and publication outside the peer-reviewed literature (LeBon, 2018 (LeBon, , 2020)). In the first peer-reviewed RCT of Stoic training, MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) assigned 45 high worriers from a university and the surrounding community to Stoic training, combined Stoic and adaptive working-memory training, or an active working-memory control condition. Both conditions containing Stoic training produced greater reductions in rumination than the active control, and Stoic training alone produced greater improvements in self-efficacy than the active control. Text analyses also indicated reductions in anxious and negatively valanced language during training, suggesting changes in cognitive-emotional processing beyond questionnaire outcomes. In a subsequent study of 24 medical students, Brown et al. (2022) observed within-group increases in Stoic attitudes and behaviors, resilience, and empathy; however, they did not employ a control group. These findings provide preliminary support for Stoic training, but larger RCTs are needed, particularly for outcomes closely tied to cognitive models of social anxiety in college students such as FNE.

Stoicism contains principles and practices that may be especially relevant to the cognitive processes maintaining FNE. Broadly, Stoic philosophy emphasizes intentional action, attention to what is under personal control, acceptance of what is outside personal control, and examination of the judgments that contribute to emotional distress. Two central Stoic principles, the distinction between controllable and uncontrollable events and the proposition that emotional responses are shaped by judgments, have substantial conceptual overlap with the cognitive model underlying cognitive and behavioral therapies (CBT) (Beck, 1976; Ellis, 1962 Ellis, , 2010;; LeBon et al., 2026; Robertson & Codd, 2019). In fact, both Ellis and Beck explicitly identified Stoic philosophy as an important precursor to rational-emotive behavior therapy and cognitive therapy, respectively, two foundational traditions within modern CBT, although these approaches subsequently developed as distinct therapeutic systems (Beck et al., 1979; Ellis, 1962 Ellis, , 2010;; Robertson, 2016). Applied to social evaluation, Stoic beliefs about control may shift attention away from attempts to manage other people's judgments and toward one's own choices and behavior (LeBon et al., 2026; Robertson & Codd, 2019). Relatedly, Stoic beliefs about happiness may weaken the assumption that favorable evaluation is necessary for well-being by treating reputation and social approval as external outcomes that are not essential to flourishing (LeBon et al., 2026; Sellars, 2006). More broadly, Stoic practices that emphasize monitoring one's judgments and evaluating oneself according to one's conduct rather than external approval may help individuals identify and reconsider catastrophic assumptions about embarrassment, rejection, or visible anxiety (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Karl, Fischer, & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; Sellars, 2006). Thus, Stoic training draws on a philosophical tradition that helped shape foundational cognitive approaches within CBT while presenting these principles within a distinct and broader philosophical and ethical framework.

Previously studied Stoic interventions have combined recurring practices and readings designed to shape how individuals anticipate, interpret, and reflect on challenging experiences. The two published peer-reviewed Stoic interventions incorporated much of the same core content, with Brown et al. (2022) additionally including an empathy module. Both interventions used three recurring daily practices: Negative Visualization, Stoic Mindfulness, and Stoic Reflectionfoot_0 . Another shared element was daily readings that introduced Stoic concepts and prompted participants to summarize, reflect on, and apply the material (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). Collectively, these components repeatedly target how individuals anticipate, interpret, and reflect on challenging experiences. Negative Visualization involves intentionally considering the possibility that an unwanted outcome could occur and preparing to cope with or respond constructively to it, rather than relying on reassurance that it will not happen (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). It therefore differs conceptually from the maladaptive anticipatory processing implicated in social anxiety, which often centers on threat, catastrophic predictions, and perceived inability to cope (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007), by pairing consideration of possible adverse outcomes with deliberate preparation for practical action and emotional coping. Stoic Mindfulness involves identifying one's judgments, distinguishing them from the events or initial impressions on which they are based, and examining the sequence of experiences and interpretations that gave rise to them. Stoic Reflection involves reviewing one's thoughts and actions from the day, identifying behaviors or responses that were unhelpful, considering opportunities or duties that were left unaddressed, recognizing what was done well, and reflecting on how one might respond more intentionally in the future. The rotating readings broaden these practices and situate them within a coherent Stoic philosophical framework by introducing additional Stoic principles and asking participants to apply them to their own experiences (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). Although these practices are designed to address stressful experiences broadly, they may be especially well suited to reducing FNE among college students, who routinely encounter situations involving social scrutiny and the possibility of unfavorable judgment. In socially evaluative contexts, these practices may weaken assumptions that embarrassment, criticism, or unfavorable judgments would be intolerable, reduce efforts to control others' impressions, and strengthen perceived capacity to respond effectively when unfavorable evaluation cannot be prevented. Across repeated practice, Stoic training may therefore reduce FNE by fostering more adaptive ways of anticipating, interpreting, and reflecting on socially evaluative experiences.

Classical Stoic texts and recent psychological evidence suggest that Negative Visualization may be particularly relevant to FNE, but the specific time course and effects on broad FNE versus acute social-evaluative stress are not clear. Negative Visualization can be applied prospectively before the precise form of an anticipated social challenge is known. In Meditations, Marcus Aurelius prepares himself to encounter difficult interpersonal behavior without knowing precisely when or how it will occur and rehearses his intended response (Meditations, 2.1). Epictetus similarly advises practitioners to consider the difficulties commonly associated with an activity before undertaking it and to prepare their response (Enchiridion, 4), while Seneca argues that adversity has a gentler impact when considered beforehand because part of its disruptive force derives from novelty (Moral Letters, 76.33-34). Consistent with this rationale, participants in a prior Stoic training intervention qualitatively described Negative Visualization as helping them anticipate difficulties, develop contingency plans, reduce uncertainty, and avoid catastrophizing when events did not proceed as expected (Brown et al., 2022). However, the effects of Negative Visualization may nevertheless differ between broad FNE and immediate acute responses to social evaluation. Across the intervention period, repeated Stoic practice may weaken relatively enduring beliefs that unfavorable evaluation would be intolerable and increase confidence in coping with negative social outcomes, consistent with preliminary evidence that Stoic training may promote preparedness and self-efficacy more broadly (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). When practiced immediately before a social stressor, Negative Visualization could similarly reduce surprise and uncertainty, increase preparedness, and thereby lessen acute emotional reactivity (Brown et al., 2022). However, contemplating possible failure could also temporarily increase threat salience and anticipatory arousal (Makkar & Grisham, 2011; Schulz et al., 2008), particularly among individuals who have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework. To our knowledge, no prior study has examined the physiological effects of a Stoic intervention. Of note, evidence that intervention-related improvements in broad FNE extend to acute reactivity during social evaluation also remains limited. For example, although online CBM-I produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE in adults than an active control at follow-up, it did not alter HR or HRV responses to a social-evaluative performance task administered after training (Abado et al., 2026). Thus, is important to determine whether Stoic training alters broad FNE, immediate subjective distress, and cardiac responses during acute social evaluation in parallel or produces divergent effects across these outcomes.

The Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) is well suited to examine acute subjective and cardiac responses. Heart rate (HR) reflects autonomic mobilization during stress, arising from increased sympathetic influence, parasympathetic withdrawal, or both, whereas heart rate variability (HRV), particularly when indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), primarily reflects parasympathetic, or vagal, modulation of the heart (Berntson et al., 1997; Laborde et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2024). Within the neurovisceral integration framework, greater resting vagally mediated HRV is associated with more flexible top-down regulation of autonomic, cognitive, and emotional responses (Thayer et al., 2009 (Thayer et al., , 2012)). Lower subjective distress accompanied by attenuated HR reactivity and greater HRV would therefore be broadly consistent with reduced stress responding and more flexible autonomic regulation (Laborde et al., 2017; Thayer et al., 2009 Thayer et al., , 2012)). However, the magnitude and direction of cardiovascular responses during acute stress do not have a one-to-one psychological interpretation. Greater HR activation during acute stress may accompany heightened threat responding, effort mobilization, or active engagement with a demanding task rather than distress alone (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Ginty et al., 2022; Seery, 2011). Likewise, lower HRV during acute stress may accompany heightened stress or threat reactivity, increased cognitive or regulatory demand, or more effortful responding during the task (Delliaux et al., 2019; Laborde et al., 2017). Comparing subjective distress with the magnitude and timing of HR and HRV responses across the TSST may therefore help distinguish whether Stoic training attenuates social-evaluative stress, alters engagement with the stressor, or produces partially divergent subjective and physiological effects.

In addition to evaluating distal psychological outcomes, it is important to determine whether Stoic training impacts the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. Prior studies have reported within-group increases in Stoic attitudes following training, but the evidence remains limited: Brown et al. (2022) did not include a control group, and MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) did not observe a statistically significant between-group difference. The recently validated Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale (SABS) was developed specifically to assess philosophical Stoicism rather than colloquial 'stoicism' (i.e., emotional suppression). Validation in more than 8,000 participants supported a 40-item measure comprising seven related dimensions: beliefs about happiness, Stoic mindfulness, virtue, benevolence and compassion, beliefs about control, ethical development, and Stoic worldview (LeBon et al., 2026). Thus, change in total SABS scores may provide an index of overall intervention target engagement, while the subscales may clarify whether changes were broadly distributed across SABS or concentrated in particular facets. Moreover, recent cross-sectional evidence linking higher SABS scores with greater well-being, resilience, self-efficacy, cognitive reappraisal, and character strengths, and with lower worry, dysfunctional attitudes, emotion-regulation difficulties, and dysfunctional anger, suggests that the Stoic attitudes and behaviors assessed by the SABS may represent a psychologically meaningful intervention target with broad relevance to mental health and well-being (Karl & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026).

The present RCT aimed to evaluate the effects of Stoic training on FNE, broader psychological functioning, SABS, and responses to acute social-evaluative stress among college students. Our primary preregistered research question was as follows: Does Stoic Training bolster resilience to social stress? Relative to the control condition, we hypothesized that Stoic training would produce lower postintervention FNE when adjusting for preintervention FNE (H1a). During the TSST, we further hypothesized lower HR (H1b), greater HRV (H1c), and lower subjective distress (H1d) when controlling for their respective baseline levels. Further, as an additional test of H1d, we also predicted a smaller pre-to post-TSST increase in state anxiety in the Stoic training group. We also preregistered hypotheses that Stoic training would reduce rumination (H2a) and increase self-efficacy (H2b) and resilience (H2c). These secondary hypotheses tested whether previously reported benefits of Stoic training for self-efficacy and rumination would replicate in a larger, exclusively undergraduate sample and whether prior within-group evidence for increased resilience would extend to a between-group RCT effect. Finally, we conducted planned exploratory analyses of the SABS total score and its seven subscales to assess intervention target engagement and identify which Stoic attitudes were most responsive to training. Overall, the study tested whether a brief, electronically delivered Stoic intervention could influence a theoretically central cognitive vulnerability, its associated acute stress response, broader psychological risk and protective factors, and the Stoic attitudes and behaviors the intervention was designed to cultivate.

Method

Transparency and Openness

Analysis code, study materials, and deidentified data are available on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/d3ex4/?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72. Stoic training materials, active control materials, and the TSST laboratory visit script are provided in Supplemental Appendices S1-S3. The study was preregistered on the OSF before data collection began: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HF4UK.

Deviations from the preregistered protocol.

Blood pressure was removed from the protocol before data collection because equipment failure prevented its acquisition. Galvanic skin response data were not analyzed because frequent electrode detachment produced unreliable signal quality and no standardized procedure was available to reliably determine which recordings were usable. For clarity of presentation, the preregistered hypotheses were reordered in the manuscript. The FNE hypothesis, preregistered as H1d, is presented as H1a, with no change to its specification or planned analysis. Further, the planned sample size was increased after additional resources allowed an extended data-collection period. This decision was made prior to analysis to maximize statistical power.

Participants

Participant flow is shown in Figure 1. Demographic characteristics of the full analytic sample and psychophysiological subsample are presented in Table 1 and Table S1, respectively. Sample size was determined by the maximum number of participants who could be recruited and tested within the available data-collection period. Enrollment Completed initial pre-training survey (n = 151) ↓ Excluded before invitation (n = 7) BRS score > 4.3 (n = 7) ↓ Invited to continue into the trial (n = 144) ↓ Declined participation (n = 23) ↓ Randomized (n = 121) ↓ ↓ Allocation Allocated to Stoic Training (n = 61) Allocated to Active Control (n = 60) ↓ ↓ Follow-up Lost to follow-up / discontinued during intervention stage (n = 15) Lost to follow-up / discontinued during control stage (n = 8) ↓ ↓ Completed post-training self-report and included in main RCT analyses (n = 46) Completed post-training self-report and included in main RCT analyses (n = 52) ↓ ↓ Invited to laboratory visit (n = 46) Withdrew / did not complete lab visit (n = 7) Completed lab visit / TSST procedures (n = 39) Invited to laboratory visit (n = 52) Withdrew / did not complete lab visit (n = 13) Completed lab visit / TSST procedures (n = 39) ↓ ↓ Analysis Excluded from primary ECG analyses because of unusable or missing ECG data (n = 7) Excluded from primary ECG analyses because of unusable or missing ECG data (n = 5) ↓ ↓ Included in primary physiological analyses (HR, HRV) (n = 32) Included in primary physiological analyses (HR, HRV) (n = 34) ↓ Phase-specific exploratory ECG analyses: usable data were available for 65-69 participants depending on phase.

Participants were 98 undergraduate students recruited via the Hamilton College online recruitment system. As compensation, participants were offered extra credit in their eligible psychology and neuroscience courses. Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect. From a total of 151 participants who completed an initial pre-training survey, 7 were excluded due to a BRS score greater than 4.3, and 144 were invited to participate in the study, of which 121 accepted. Of those 121, 23 voluntarily dropped out during the intervention or control stage, leading to a final RCT sample of 98 participants providing self-report data at pre-training and post-training. Participants were randomly allocated to either Stoic Training (pre-training n = 61, post-training n = 46) or Active Control (pre-training n = 60, post-training n = 52). Groups did not significantly vary on age, biological sex, gender, first generation student status, subjective social status, or race/ethnicity (see Supplement for details) nor did they vary on any pre-training self-report measures (see Table 2). However, pre-training subjective social status relative to the country as a whole (p = .061) and first-generation status (p = .072) were trending towards significance (see Supplement).

All 98 participants who completed the post-training survey were invited to participate in a lab visit, of whom 78 completed a lab visit (n = 39 Stoic, n = 39 Control). For our preregistered analyses of heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV), usable electrocardiography (ECG) data were available for 66 of the 78 participants who visited the lab (84.6%; n = 32 Stoic, n = 34 Control). For phase-specific exploratory analyses, usable data were available for 65-69 participants (83.3%-88.5%; see Supplement for details). For STAI-S and SUDS, data were available for all 78 participants who completed the lab visit.

Study Design and Procedure

Participants first completed an online survey containing self-report questionnaires and demographic information. Participants who met eligibility criteria were then randomized to either the Stoic or Control condition and sent an online access link for their assigned condition. Participants were not informed that the study involved multiple experimental conditions or that they were receiving an intervention. Instead, they were told that the study examined associations between responses to daily writing prompts, stress reactivity, and resilience. The full study design was disclosed during debriefing after completion of the laboratory session. The mean number of training days participants took to complete the eight sessions of Stoic training was 11.39 days, SD = 3.16, with the median number of days being 11. After completing the training period, participants completed the same self-report questionnaires administered at baseline. Participants were then invited to schedule a laboratory visit and were encouraged to attend within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities. When scheduling within this window was not feasible, later visits were permitted to maximize participant retention. The mean interval between completion of the assigned activities and the laboratory visit was 3.82 calendar days (median = 3, range = 1-21). Of the 82 laboratory attendees, 23 (28.0%) attended more than four calendar days after completion. Accordingly, sensitivity analyses repeated the preregistered laboratory outcome models with the number of calendar days between completion and the laboratory visit included as an additional covariate. Prior to the lab visit, participants were asked to refrain from caffeine for 6 hours, alcohol for 12 hours, and food and vigorous exercise for 3 hours. During the lab visit, participants completed brief pre-task questionnaires to measure adherence to protocol and baseline state anxiety. After completing self-report forms, participants were connected to physiological recording equipment, completed a modified TSST, and self-reported post-TSST state anxiety.

Pre-task questionnaires revealed that one participant reported caffeine consumption within 6 hours of their lab visit and one reported vigorous exercise within 3 hours of their lab visit; no participants reported food consumption within 3 hours or alcohol consumption within 12 hours. Sensitivity analyses were run to account for deviations from protocol.

Intervention and Control Conditions

The Stoic training was delivered online following procedures established in MacLellan & Derakshan (2021). Briefly, participants in the Stoic condition completed 8 daily training sessions. Participants were instructed to complete the eight sessions within 12 days, although additional time was permitted when necessary. The 8 daily sessions consisted of three recurring daily activities: Negative Visualization, Stoic Mindfulness, and Stoic Reflection; participants in the Stoic condition also read and summarized a daily Stoic reading for each of the 8 days. The daily reading changed each day and included passages of Stoic text followed by instructions to summarize their thoughts about the passages. By contrast, the active control entailed reading literary fiction passages followed by instructions to summarize and reflect on those passages. All training materials were delivered via Qualtrics and the full Stoic training and active control materials can be found in the Supplement.

Materials and Tasks

Self-report Questionnaires

Participants completed the Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale to measure Stoicism as a life philosophy (SABS; LeBon et al., 2026), Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale to measure fear of negative evaluation (BFNE; Leary 1983), the Ruminative Response Scale-10 to measure rumination (RRS-10; Treynor et al., 2003), the General Self-Efficacy Scale to measure selfefficacy (GSE; Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995), the Brief Resilience Scale to measure resilience as the ability to bounce back from stress (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10 to measure resilience as perceived ability to cope with and adapt to adversity (CD-RISC-10; Campbell-Sills and Stein 2007). Baseline Subjective Social Status was measured using the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status (MacArthur SSS Scale; Adler et al. (2000). Internal-consistency estimates for all multi-item self-report measures are reported in Table S6, with corresponding estimates for the SABS subscales reported in Table S7 of the Supplement.

Trier Social Stress Test

Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993), a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat. The task followed standard TSST procedures with one additional phase: a 5-minute intervention/control phase was added immediately before speech preparation. During this phase, participants assigned to Stoic training were instructed to apply the practice of Negative Visualization to the upcoming social stress task during a 5-minute period, whereas participants assigned to the control condition were instructed to wait quietly for 5 minutes. The full task sequence consisted of a 5-minute seated baseline, 5-minute intervention/control phase, 5minute speech preparation period, 5-minute speech, 5-minute mental arithmetic task, and 5minute recovery period. For the speech task, participants were instructed to give a speech about why they were qualified for their dream job in front of two evaluative panelists. For the mental arithmetic task, participants were instructed to serially subtract 13 from 1,022 as quickly and accurately as possible and to start over if they made an error. Physiological measures were recorded continuously throughout the task. Participants remained seated throughout the procedure and were instructed to remain as still as possible during physiological recording. TSST panelists were aware of condition assignment because the laboratory procedure included a condition-specific intervention/control phase immediately before speech preparation. The full standardized TSST script can be found in the Supplement.

Physiological Data Acquisition and Processing

Electrocardiography (ECG) was recorded continuously using a Biopac MP36R data acquisition system (Biopac Systems, Inc., Goleta, CA). ECG was recorded from three Ag/AgCl electrodes; one electrode was placed below the right clavicle in the second intercostal space, and one electrode was placed on each lower rib cage in the eighth intercostal space. ECG data were acquired at a sampling rate of 1,000 Hz, amplified, and digitized using the Biopac MP36R system. Electrodes were also placed on the palms to record galvanic skin response (GSR). However, for GSR, frequent electrode detachment resulted in unreliable signal quality, and no standardized procedure was available to determine consistently which participants had provided usable recordings. GSR data were therefore not processed or analyzed. Although blood pressure was included in the preregistered protocol, it was removed before data collection because equipment failure prevented its acquisition. ECG data were segmented into six 5-min phases: baseline, intervention/control, speech preparation, speech, mental arithmetic, and recovery. ECG data were processed and screened prior to hypothesis testing and blind to participant condition. ECG data were high-pass filtered at 3 Hz and low-pass filtered at 35 Hz. The 3-Hz lower cutoff was consistent with prior ECG preprocessing in TSST research before QRS detection and RR-interval calculation (Ringgold et al., 2025), while low-pass cutoffs of approximately 35-40 Hz have been commonly used in ECG preprocessing (e.g., Tejedor et al., 2019). R-peaks were identified in AcqKnowledge and were visually inspected for signal quality. Segments with recording failures or unusable signal quality were removed following visual inspection. Continuous RR interval data and event markers were exported for further processing. In R, RR intervals were flagged as invalid if they were physiologically implausible (<0.30 s or >2.00 s) or deviated by more than 30% from an 11-beat rolling median. Flagged RR intervals were visually inspected and then set to missing. Five-minute segments were treated as missing when 10% or more of RR intervals within that segment were invalid. Applying these criteria, usable HR and HRV data were available for 69 participants during baseline, intervention/control, speech preparation, and speech; 66 participants during mental arithmetic; and 65 participants during recovery. HR was calculated as 60 divided by the mean RR interval within each phase. HRV was operationalized as the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), calculated from RR intervals within each 5-min phase and natural-log transformed prior to analysis (Laborde et al., 2017).

State Measures

State anxiety was assessed using the state subscale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S; Spielberger et al., 1983). The STAI-S was administered immediately before and after the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) to assess changes in state anxiety associated with the stressor. Momentary subjective distress was assessed using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS; Wolpe, 1969). Participants rated their current level of distress on a scale ranging from 0 (no distress at all) to 100 (the most distress imaginable), with higher ratings indicating greater subjective distress. SUDS ratings were obtained at the following 6 timepoints: prior to baseline, after baseline, after intervention/control, after speech preparation, after TSST, after recovery.

Analysis

All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2026). Unless otherwise specified, tests were two-tailed with α = .05. To evaluate whether the modified TSST successfully elicited stressrelated changes, we conducted manipulation-check models comparing HR, HRV, and SUDS across baseline, TSST, and recovery. For HR and HRV, TSST values were averaged across the speech and mental-arithmetic phases. Manipulation checks were conducted using linear mixed-effects models estimated with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015), with phase entered as a within-participant fixed effect and a random intercept for participant.

Primary preregistered hypotheses were tested using linear regression models with group assignment as the predictor of interest and baseline levels of the outcome measure included as a covariate. Thus, for preregistered self-report outcomes, separate models tested Stoic training effects on post-treatment FNE, rumination, self-efficacy, and resilience while controlling for the corresponding pretreatment score. SABS was analyzed using an analogous baseline-adjusted regression model with post-treatment SABS as the dependent variable, group assignment as the predictor of interest, and baseline SABS as a covariate. For preregistered TSST outcomes, separate models tested Stoic training effects on HR, HRV, and SUDS while controlling for the corresponding baseline score. The TSST-average physiology variables were computed from the speech and mental-arithmetic phases and required valid data from both phases. State anxiety was examined using the preregistered one-tailed independent-samples t test, with change in STAI-S from pre-to post-TSST compared between conditions. For regression models, adjusted standardized mean differences were calculated by dividing the condition coefficient by the model residual standard deviation (Hedges et al., 2023). For STAI-S, Cohen's d represented the standardized between-condition difference in change scores.

Preregistered GSR and blood-pressure analyses were not conducted because bloodpressure equipment failure prevented data collection and GSR signal quality could not be evaluated reliably.

Exploratory analyses were conducted to characterize SABS subscales, within-group change in self-report outcomes, and the time course of physiological effects. Paired-samples t tests examined pre-to post-treatment change separately within the Stoic and control groups for each self-report outcome. Following the same analytic approach used for the preregistered selfreport analyses, analogous exploratory baseline-adjusted regression models tested Stoic training effects on SABS subscales. Exploratory linear regressions also tested condition differences in baseline HR and HRV. To clarify the phase-specific pattern of physiological effects, separate baseline-adjusted regressions tested Stoic training effects on HR and HRV during the intervention/control, speech-preparation, speech, mental-arithmetic, and recovery phases. In addition, exploratory linear mixed-effects models included the fixed effects of condition, phase, and their interaction, with participant included as a random intercept. Follow-up contrasts, estimated using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026), tested group differences at each phase and whether baseline-relative changes differed by condition. Phase-specific regressions included participants with valid baseline and outcome data for the relevant phase, whereas mixed-effects models used all available valid phase-level observations.

To control the familywise error rate, Hommel adjustments were applied separately within prespecified families of exploratory tests (Hommel, 1988). The within-condition pre-to posttreatment comparisons formed one family within the Stoic condition and one family within the control condition. All seven SABS subscale regression models formed one family. The phasespecific regression models formed separate families for HR, HRV, and SUDS, with the postbaseline phases corrected within each outcome. Follow-up between-condition comparisons derived from the mixed-effects models also formed separate families for HR, HRV, and SUDS.

Sensitivity Analyses and Missing data

Prior to hypothesis testing, we examined baseline differences between the Stoic training and control groups on pre-treatment self-report outcomes and demographics. In cases of significant differences or meeting our prespecified p < .1 sensitivity analysis criterion, we conducted sensitivity analyses with those variables included as covariates. Thus, for self-report outcomes, sensitivity analyses were performed by repeating pre-registered regression analyses with the addition of subjective social status relative to the country as a covariate and then separately with first generation status as a covariate. For TSST outcomes, we repeated preregistered regression analyses with the addition of subjective social status relative to the country as a covariate.

Additional sensitivity analyses evaluated laboratory timing and deviations from the intended laboratory protocol. Participants were encouraged to attend the laboratory visit within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities, although later visits were permitted when scheduling within this window was not feasible. To evaluate whether variability in visit timing affected the findings, the preregistered TSST outcome models were repeated with the number of calendar days between completion of the assigned activities and the laboratory visit included as an additional covariate. In a separate protocol-adherence analysis, the preregistered TSST models were repeated after excluding two participants: one who reported consuming caffeine within six hours of the laboratory visit and one who reported engaging in vigorous exercise within three hours of the laboratory visit.

Missingness was evaluated separately for self-report outcomes and TSST outcomes. Attrition for post-training self-report outcomes was evaluated among participants with identifiable Day 1 training data. We examined whether completion of the intervention and subsequent post-training assessment differed by condition and whether it was associated with baseline SABS, FNE, CD-RISC, BRS, GSE, or RRS scores. To evaluate the robustness of the preregistered self-report outcome findings to missing data, the baseline-adjusted models were repeated using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011). The imputation model included condition and baseline and post-training values for the preregistered self-report outcomes. Fifty imputed datasets were generated over 20 iterations using predictive mean matching, and estimates were pooled using Rubin's (1987) rules.

For HR and HRV, phase-specific data availability was summarized, and Little's MCAR test (Little, 1988) was conducted among participants with at least one usable physiological observation using baseline, speech, and mental-arithmetic HR, HRV, and SUDS values. We also examined whether the availability of usable physiological data differed by condition. As a sensitivity analysis, the preregistered TSST models were repeated using TSST averages calculated from whichever of the speech and mental-arithmetic phases was available. Given the limited missingness for TSST outcomes, they were not multiply imputed.

Results

Participant Characteristics and Preliminary Analyses
