Preregistered Research Question 1: Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress

Fear of Negative Evaluation

In support of preregistered Hypothesis 1a, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining fear of negative evaluation after adjustment for pretraining BFNE scores, b = -2.77, SE = 1.13, t(95) = -2.45, p = .016, 95% CI [-5.01, -0.53], adjusted d = -0.50. Consistent with this effect, BFNE scores decreased within the Stoic training condition from pre-to posttraining, mean change = -2.76, 95% CI [-4.57, -0.95], p = .004, Hommel-adjusted p = .012, whereas the control condition showed no significant change, mean change = -0.19, 95% CI [-1.61, 1.22], p = .786.

Subjective Responses to the TSST

Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1b, Stoic training was not associated with lower subjective distress during the TSST. After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.

The preregistered analysis of state anxiety also did not support the hypothesized effect. Although the mean increase in STAI-S scores from before to after the TSST was smaller in the Stoic training condition (2.65 points) than in the control condition (5.41 points), the preregistered onetailed Welch's t test did not indicate a significant between-condition difference, t(63.92) = 1.24, p = .109, adjusted d = -.29.

Cardiac Responses to the TSST

Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1c, Stoic training was associated with higher rather than lower heart rate during the TSST after adjustment for baseline heart rate, b = 4.13, SE = 1.95, t(63) = 2.12, p = .038, 95% CI [0.24, 8.02], adjusted d = 0.53.

Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1d, the estimated effect on heart-rate variability was also opposite to the hypothesized direction. After adjustment for baseline HRV, Stoic training was associated with lower HRV during the TSST, although the effect narrowly missed the preregistered threshold for statistical significance, b = -0.17, SE = 0.08, t(63) = -1.97, p = .053, 95% CI [-0.335, 0.002], adjusted d = -0.49.

Thus, Stoic training was associated with lower broad FNE, but it did not produce the hypothesized attenuation of subjective or cardiac responses to acute social evaluation. Figure 4 summarizes the preregistered findings for Research Question 1. Note. Points represent standardized Stoic-minus-control effect sizes. Negative values indicate lower values in the Stoic condition, whereas positive values indicate higher values. For FNE, SUDS, heart rate, and HRV, adjusted d was calculated as the baseline-adjusted Stoic coefficient divided by the model residual standard deviation. The STAI-S effect is the standardized between-condition difference in pre-to post-TSST change, with more negative values indicating a greater decrease in STAI-S. Whiskers represent 95% confidence intervals. Reported p values are two-sided except for STAI-S, which is one-sided. HRV = heart rate variability; SUDS = Subjective Units of Distress Scale; STAI-S = State-Trait Anxiety Inventory-State; FNE = fear of negative evaluation.

Preregistered Research Question 2: Resilience, Self-Efficacy, and Rumination

Findings from the preregistered baseline-adjusted regression models are presented in Table 3. Stoic training was not significantly associated with posttraining CD-RISC scores, b = 1.02, SE = 0.68, t = 1.50, p = .138, adjusted d = 0.31; BRS scores, b = 0.57, SE = 0.58, t = 0.99, p = .325, adjusted d = 0.20; GSE scores, b = -0.14, SE = 0.54, t = -0.25, p = .800, adjusted d = -0.05; or RRS scores, b = 0.52, SE = 0.91, t = 0.58, p = .566, adjusted d = 0.12, when controlling for the corresponding pretraining scores. Preregistered Hypotheses 2a-2c were therefore not supported.

Within the Stoic training condition, both CD-RISC and BRS scores increased from pre-to posttraining, and these changes remained significant after Hommel correction for multiple comparisons. CD-RISC scores also increased within the control condition at the p < .05 significance threshold, but this change did not survive correction. GSE and RRS scores did not change significantly within either condition. See Table 2 for detailed statistics from within-group analyses.

Planned Analyses of Intervention Target Engagement

SABS Total Score

Stoic training was associated with higher posttraining SABS scores after adjustment for pretraining SABS scores, b = 6.06, SE = 2.88, t(95) = 2.11, p = .038, 95% CI [0.35, 11.78], adjusted d = 0.43. Consistent with this effect, SABS scores increased within the Stoic training condition from pre-to posttraining, mean change = 7.67, 95% CI [2.76, 12.58], p = .003, Hommel-adjusted p = .012, whereas the control condition showed no significant change, mean change = 0.90, 95% CI [-2.42, 4.23], p = .587.

SABS Subscales

Exploratory baseline-adjusted regression models examined condition differences across the seven SABS subscales (Table 4). Stoic training was associated with higher posttraining Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness scores after adjustment for the corresponding pretraining scores. However, neither association remained statistically significant after Hommel correction across the seven subscale models, and no other baseline-adjusted between-condition effect was significant.

Complementary within-condition analyses are presented in Table S2.

Within the Stoic training condition, Beliefs About Control and Stoic Worldview increased from pre-to posttraining and remained significant after Hommel correction. Stoic Mindfulness also increased at the p < .05 significance threshold but did not survive correction. Within the control condition, Beliefs About Happiness decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold but did not remain significant after correction. No other within-condition changes were statistically significant.

Exploratory Analyses of Laboratory Response Trajectories

Exploratory mixed-effects models were used to examine whether condition differences varied across the full TSST time course. Significant Condition × Phase interactions emerged for both heart rate, F(5, 328.02) = 2.83, p = .016, and HRV, F(5, 328.10) = 2.81, p = .017.

Follow-up contrasts comparing change from baseline across conditions indicated that Stoic training participants exhibited a larger increase in HR from baseline to speech, b = 4.37, SE = 1.65, t = 2.66, raw p = .008, Hommel-adjusted p = .041. Stoic training participants also exhibited a larger decrease in HRV from baseline to speech, b = -0.21, SE = 0.08, t = -2.69, raw p = .008, Hommel-adjusted p = .036. The condition difference in HRV change from baseline to mental arithmetic was significant before correction, raw p = .022, but did not survive Hommel correction, adjusted p = .066. The corresponding recovery contrast was also significant before correction, raw p = .021, but not afterward, adjusted p = .062. No other change-from-baseline contrast was significant after correction.

Complementary phase-specific regressions adjusting for baseline values indicated that Stoic training was associated with higher HR during the intervention, speech, and recovery phases and with lower HRV during speech and recovery. After applying Hommel corrections separately within the HR and HRV phase-specific model families, only the association between Stoic training and lower HRV during recovery remained statistically significant, b = -0.18, SE = 0.06, t = -3.11, raw p = .003, Hommel-adjusted p = .014. Stoic training was not significantly associated with baseline HR or HRV. Full phase-specific results are presented in Table S3.

The Condition × Phase interaction for SUDS was not statistically significant, F(5, 386.41) = 1.73, p = .126. Follow-up contrast suggested that Stoic training participants exhibited a larger increase from pre-baseline to post-TSST when evaluating significance at the p < .05 level, b = 7.40, SE = 3.62, t = 2.04, raw p = .042, but this effect did not remain significant after Hommel correction, adjusted p = .175. Baseline-adjusted phase-specific regressions likewise found no significant condition difference in SUDS at any assessment after correction. Estimated marginal means, change-from-baseline contrasts, and simple between-condition comparisons are reported in Tables S4 and S5.

Sensitivity and Missing-Data Analyses

Full sensitivity and missing-data analyses are reported in the Supplement. Sensitivity analyses adjusting separately for first-generation status and subjective social status relative to the United States produced effects that were consistent in direction and generally consistent in magnitude with the preregistered models. All findings that were statistically significant in the primary analyses remained significant after covariate adjustment. The estimated HRV effect, which narrowly missed significance in the primary model, reached statistical significance after adjustment for subjective social status, p = .043. When excluding the two participants who reported deviations from laboratory preparation requirements, the HR effect remained significant and the HRV effect reached statistical significance, p = .043. Adjustment for the interval between training completion and the laboratory visit also did not meaningfully alter the TSST findings: the HR effect remained significant, p = .045, the HRV effect remained similar in magnitude but nonsignificant, p = .062, and the interval itself was unrelated to the laboratory outcomes, all ps ≥ .360.

Posttraining completion did not differ significantly by condition, and no baseline self-report variable was significantly associated with completion after correction for multiple comparisons.

In multiple-imputation analyses, the estimated effect of Stoic training on FNE remained statistically significant. The estimated effect of Stoic training on SABS remained positive and similar in magnitude to the complete-case estimate but was no longer statistically significant in the primary imputed analysis, p = .075, indicating that inference regarding SABS target engagement was somewhat sensitive to the treatment of missing posttraining data.

Physiological and laboratory self-report missingness was limited, compatible with data missing completely at random, and unrelated to condition. HR and HRV findings were also robust when TSST averages were calculated using whichever of the speech and mental-arithmetic phases was available. Under this specification, the effect of Stoic training on HR remained significant, p = .027, and the effect on HRV reached statistical significance, p = .022.

Discussion

The present study examined whether a brief, digitally delivered Stoic training intervention could reduce FNE, alter broader psychological outcomes, increase Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and influence subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress. Stoic training was associated with a moderate reduction in broad FNE relative to an active control, and this effect remained evident across sensitivity analyses addressing baseline characteristics and missing posttraining data. To our knowledge, this is the first RCT to demonstrate that a digitally delivered intervention can produce a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE than an active control among college students when administered during an ongoing academic semester. Stoic training was also associated with higher posttraining SABS scores in the complete-case analysis. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate a significant between-condition increase in the attitudes and behaviors targeted by Stoic training, although this finding was less robust to the treatment of missing data. By contrast, betweencondition differences in resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not statistically significant. Finally, the laboratory findings did not support the hypothesis that Stoic training would attenuate acute social-evaluative stress responses. Cardiac effects were instead opposite to prediction, with Stoic training associated with higher HR and lower HRV during the TSST, whereas subjective distress and state-anxiety responses did not differ significantly between conditions. Together, these findings suggest that brief Stoic training may reduce broad FNE and increase Stoic attitudes and behaviors, while effects on the other psychological outcomes assessed here were more limited and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress were amplified rather than attenuated.

The reduction in FNE is particularly notable given the limited evidence that brief or scalable interventions reduce broad FNE relative to active comparison conditions in college populations (Hoppitt et al., 2014; Zaboski et al., 2019). The present findings extend prior work by showing that a brief, digitally delivered intervention can produce a between-condition reduction in broad FNE, when compared to an active control, while students are already navigating ongoing academic and interpersonal demands. This complements earlier evidence from interventions delivered before or around the transition to college (Hoppitt et al., 2014), while also addressing a more ecologically typical period in which social-evaluative concerns are already embedded in day-to-day academic and social life (Campbell et al., 2016). More broadly, the findings add to evidence that FNE may be modifiable through relatively brief cognitive interventions (Arai et al., 2023; Hoppitt et al., 2014; McCall et al., 2018), while suggesting that a broad philosophical training approach can influence this vulnerability even when it is not designed as a disorder-specific treatment.

The FNE finding is consistent with the possibility that Stoic training may have altered appraisals that are especially relevant to social evaluation. In particular, the intervention may have reduced the perceived importance or intolerability of others' judgments, or increased confidence in coping with unfavorable evaluation, consistent with cognitive models emphasizing maladaptive beliefs about social evaluation and its consequences (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). This interpretation is supported indirectly by the concurrent increase in total SABS scores in the primary complete-case analysis, suggesting that reductions in FNE occurred alongside greater endorsement of the Stoic attitudes and behaviors targeted by the intervention. At the same time, the present study did not test, nor was designed with sufficient timepoints and statistical power to test, whether changes in SABS mediated the FNE effect, and the reduction in FNE cannot be attributed to any specific Stoic facet or practice. Future work should employ longitudinal designs with three or more measurement occasions to establish temporal ordering (Maxwell & Cole, 2007) and test whether changes in Stoic attitudes, perceived controllability, catastrophic beliefs about social evaluation, coping confidence, anticipatory processing, or impression-management efforts mediate subsequent reductions in FNE.

The increase in total SABS scores is also important given the growing interest in Stoic training as a psychological intervention and emerging evidence that the attitudes and behaviors captured by the SABS are meaningfully associated with mental health and well-being. Higher SABS scores have recently been linked cross-sectionally with greater well-being, resilience, selfefficacy, character strengths, and cognitive reappraisal, as well as lower worry, dysfunctional attitudes, emotion-regulation difficulties, and dysfunctional anger (Karl & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026), suggesting that Stoic attitudes may represent a potentially meaningful intervention target rather than merely a marker of philosophical identification. Against this background, the present between-condition effect is notable because prior intervention studies have provided only within-group evidence of change in Stoic attitudes or have failed to detect a significant controlled effect (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021). To our knowledge, the present study therefore provides the first RCT evidence that Stoic training can produce a significant increase in SABS scores relative to a control condition. This finding provides preliminary support for the malleability of Stoic attitudes under experimental conditions and strengthens the rationale for treating SABS as an intervention target in future Stoic training research. At the same time, the effect should be interpreted cautiously: although its direction and approximate magnitude were similar under multiple imputation, it no longer reached statistical significance when missing posttraining data were imputed. Replication in larger samples will therefore be important for establishing the robustness of the betweencondition effect.

Exploratory analyses further suggested that some dimensions of Stoic attitudes may be more responsive to brief training than others. To our knowledge, this is also the first study to examine intervention-related change across individual SABS subscales, providing an initial indication of which facets of Stoic attitudes may be most malleable under brief training. Baseline-adjusted between-condition effects were nominally significant for Beliefs About Happiness and Beliefs About Control, although neither remained significant following correction for multiple comparisons. Within the Stoic condition, Beliefs About Control and Stoic Worldview increased and were significant after correction, with a smaller uncorrected increase in Stoic Mindfulness. These exploratory findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence that Stoic training selectively changes particular SABS facets. They are also necessarily specific to the content of the present intervention and the population studied. Other forms of Stoic training may place greater emphasis on different philosophical principles and may therefore produce different profiles of change across SABS dimensions. Future research could examine whether particular intervention components preferentially target specific SABS facets and whether those facets, in turn, are differentially associated with particular psychological outcomes or populations. Such work could eventually inform more targeted or personalized Stoic interventions, in which training components are selected according to the attitudes most relevant to a given psychological vulnerability, population, or intervention goal. In the present study, Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness may warrant particular attention because both are theoretically relevant to FNE: Stoic beliefs about control emphasize directing effort toward one's own actions rather than other people's evaluations, whereas Stoic beliefs about happiness challenge the assumption that reputation or social approval is necessary for well-being (Clark & Wells, 1995; LeBon et al., 2026; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997). Larger longitudinal trials could determine whether changes in these facets reliably occur following training and whether they mediate reductions in FNE or other psychological outcomes.

In contrast to the FNE findings, the preregistered hypotheses concerning self-efficacy, rumination, and resilience were not supported. For self-efficacy and rumination, the present findings did not replicate the previously reported between-condition improvements following Stoic training (MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021), underscoring the need for additional studies to establish potential boundary conditions. Of note, MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) recruited individuals selected for high worry from a university and surrounding community, whereas the present study involved a general undergraduate sample, potentially leaving less scope for improvement on some outcomes. Regarding resilience, Brown et al. (2022) previously reported a within-group increase in resilience as measured using the BRS among medical students receiving Stoic training. Consistent with that finding, the present study found significant increases in resilience as measured by the BRS and CD-RISC within the Stoic training group, both of which survived correction for multiple comparisons. However, the present study extends that earlier work by including an active control and found no significant between-condition effect on either resilience measure. This distinction highlights the importance of separating pre-to-post improvement within an intervention group from evidence that change exceeds what occurs under a comparison condition. Taken as a whole, our findings are consistent with the possibility that FNE may represent a comparatively proximal target of the particular Stoic principles emphasized in the present intervention, whereas resilience, general self-efficacy, and rumination are broader constructs that may require greater intervention exposure, specific target populations, and/or additional opportunities to apply Stoic practices across contexts. At the same time, the present null findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that Stoic training has no effect on these constructs. Rather, this study did not provide evidence that the present brief intervention produced detectable between-condition changes in these broader outcomes, measured immediately post-training, in this sample. Replication across larger and more diverse samples, longer training periods, and follow-up assessments will be important for determining the breadth and durability of psychological change following Stoic training.

The laboratory findings provide a different and more complex picture. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine physiological responses to acute stress following a Stoic intervention. Contrary to prediction, participants assigned to Stoic training exhibited higher baseline-adjusted HR during the TSST and lower baseline-adjusted HRV, although the preregistered HRV effect narrowly missed the conventional significance threshold. Exploratory time-course analyses further indicated greater baseline-to-speech increases in HR and decreases in HRV among participants in the Stoic condition, with both contrasts remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Notably, the conditions did not differ in baseline HR or HRV, indicating that the cardiac divergence emerged during the subsequent laboratory challenge rather than reflecting pre-existing differences at the start of the session. These findings do not support the hypothesis that Stoic training attenuates cardiac mobilization during social-evaluative stress. Importantly, however, the greater cardiac response was not accompanied by significantly greater subjective distress or state-anxiety responding. The physiological findings therefore should not be interpreted as evidence of a straightforward increase in experienced distress.

Several interpretations of this pattern remain possible. Although higher HR and lower HRV are characteristic of acute stress responding, neither response has a uniquely negative psychological meaning, and cardiac autonomic activity should not be reduced to a simple continuum from parasympathetic "calm" to sympathetic "stress" (Berntson et al., 1993 (Berntson et al., , 1997)). Depending on context, elevated HR and lower HRV during acute stress may be either adaptive or maladaptive (e.g., Laborde et al., 2017; Seery, 2011). Greater HR activation and vagal withdrawal could reflect heightened threat or stress responding, but they could also accompany greater effort mobilization, task engagement, or regulatory demand during a challenging performance (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2011). In the present study, one possibility is that applying Negative Visualization immediately before the TSST increased the salience of possible failure or negative evaluation, temporarily increasing anticipatory mobilization even if repeated Stoic practice had reduced broader beliefs about the consequences of unfavorable evaluation. This interpretation would be consistent with evidence that contemplating potential negative outcomes can sometimes increase anticipatory arousal (Makkar & Grisham, 2011; Schulz et al., 2008), an effect that may be particularly likely when individuals have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework. In this sense, Negative Visualization may initially have produced a paradoxical effect opposite to its intended regulatory function. Analogous responses have been documented during relaxation-based practices, in which attempts to reduce arousal can paradoxically increase anxiety in some individuals (Heide & Borkovec, 1984; Kim & Newman, 2019). Alternatively, Stoic training participants may have engaged more actively with the performance task or exerted greater regulatory effort without experiencing correspondingly greater subjective distress. From this perspective, greater acute cardiac activation need not indicate a detrimental response and could instead accompany more active engagement with a challenging experience. Consistent with this interpretation, greater HR reactivity to acute psychological stress has prospectively predicted better subsequent academic performance, suggesting that larger cardiac responses can accompany adaptive engagement or performance rather than distress alone (Ginty et al., 2022). This possibility is also broadly consistent with exposure-based models in which therapeutic benefit does not require low levels of distress during the challenging experience itself but may emerge through sustained engagement and new learning in the presence of distress (Craske et al., 2014; Rupp et al., 2017). However, the present measures cannot distinguish among these possibilities, and the dissociation between cardiac and subjective responses underscores that greater physiological activation should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of a more adverse stress response. Future work incorporating broader cardiovascular indices, ideally incorporating measures such as Total Peripheral Resistance to distinguish threat from challenge (Seery, 2011), alongside additional subjective and behavioral measures, will be needed to determine whether the observed pattern reflects heightened threat, greater task engagement, increased regulatory effort, or some combination of these processes.

The recovery-period findings also warrant attention. In the exploratory phase-specific baseline-adjusted regression analyses, lower HRV in the Stoic condition remained evident during recovery, and this was the only phase-specific cardiac difference to remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Although this finding should be interpreted cautiously, the persistence of lower HRV after the active stressor had ended is more consistent with sustained autonomic activation or slower vagal recovery than with an effect limited to transient task engagement during the speech itself. This pattern is therefore consistent with the possibility that Negative Visualization had a paradoxical stress-enhancing effect in this sample of novice Stoic practitioners. At the same time, the present design cannot determine whether the recovery pattern reflects a more prolonged threat response or lingering autonomic activation associated with greater engagement during the preceding task. Future studies should examine recovery slope more directly using a longer recovery period and repeated post-stressor assessments.

A critical limitation of the laboratory design is that the effects of the broader Stoic intervention cannot be separated from those of the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered immediately before speech preparation. The acute exercise was included to increase sensitivity to potential intervention-related differences in stress responding by reactivating a core Stoic practice immediately before the social-evaluative challenge, particularly given the absence of a pretreatment laboratory stress assessment. However, this design choice also complicates interpretation of the resulting condition differences. Participants in the Stoic condition had completed eight sessions of internet-delivered Stoic training and then engaged in five minutes of Negative Visualization immediately before receiving the speech instructions, whereas control participants completed eight sessions of the active control and spent the corresponding five-minute period waiting quietly. Consequently, the greater cardiac response could reflect the cumulative effects of Stoic training, the immediate effects of Negative Visualization, differences produced by the contrasting pre-stressor activities themselves, or an interaction among these factors. In particular, the quiet waiting period may have afforded control participants additional physiological acclimatization or settling immediately before the stressor, whereas Negative Visualization may have maintained or increased anticipatory activation (Hastrup, 1986; Laborde et al., 2017). Future studies should experimentally separate the repeated and acute components, for example using a factorial design in which prior Stoic training and immediate pre-stressor Negative Visualization are independently manipulated. Such a design could determine whether repeated training alters acute stress responding, whether immediate Negative Visualization has distinct effects among trained and untrained individuals, and whether the timing of Negative Visualization influences its consequences.

Beyond the laboratory design considerations discussed above, several additional limitations should be considered alongside the study's methodological strengths. The study used a preregistered randomized design with an active comparison condition and a substantially larger sample than prior peer-reviewed evaluations of Stoic training, providing greater precision for estimating between-condition effects. It also assessed both intervention outcomes and target engagement, incorporated subjective and physiological measures of acute social-evaluative responding, and made study materials, analysis code, and deidentified data openly available. Sensitivity analyses further indicated that the principal FNE finding was robust to adjustment for baseline characteristics and to multiple imputation for missing posttraining data. The focus on undergraduates was also a strength insofar as college students are a population of particular relevance to the mental health concerns motivating the study; however, the single-college, predominantly female sample limits generalizability to students at other institutions and to nonstudent adults. Attrition occurred between enrollment and posttraining assessment, and although completion did not differ significantly by condition and the FNE effect remained significant following multiple imputation, missing data introduce additional uncertainty. The inlab sample was smaller than the self-report sample, limiting precision for TSST measures, and the absence of a pretreatment laboratory stress assessment prevented examination of intervention-related change in stress reactivity from before to after training. Although there was some variability in the training-to-laboratory interval, the interval was not associated with the laboratory outcomes, and adjusting for it did not meaningfully alter the findings. The intervention also did not directly assess the cognitive processes hypothesized to account for reductions in FNE, precluding conclusions regarding mechanism or mediation. Finally, outcomes were assessed only immediately following training, leaving unclear whether reductions in FNE and changes in Stoic attitudes persist or translate into behavioral and functional improvements over time. Replication in larger and more diverse samples, with longer-term follow-up and more direct assessment of hypothesized mechanisms, will therefore be important.

Overall, the present findings provide initial evidence that a brief, digitally delivered Stoic training can reduce broad FNE relative to an active control in college students and may increase the Stoic attitudes and behaviors the intervention is intended to cultivate. These effects did not extend to significant between-condition improvements in broader measures of resilience, selfefficacy, or rumination, and reductions in FNE were not accompanied by attenuated subjective or cardiac responses to acute social evaluation. Instead, Stoic training combined with immediate Negative Visualization was associated with greater cardiac mobilization during the TSST. These divergent findings underscore the importance of distinguishing changes in relatively enduring cognitive vulnerabilities from immediate responses to acute stress and of considering the timing and context in which specific Stoic practices are applied. Further research should determine which components of Stoic training drive reductions in FNE, establish whether these effects persist over time, and disentangle the cumulative effects of repeated Stoic practice from the acute effects of Negative Visualization. If replicated and extended, these findings may establish a foundation for the further development of brief digital Stoic training as a scalable approach for targeting fear of negative evaluation in college populations, while also advancing a more nuanced understanding of how Stoic practices influence both enduring cognitive vulnerabilities and acute stress responding.
